what_its_for: Interferon beta-1b is used to treat relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (MS). It helps reduce the number of MS flare-ups (relapses) and may slow down the worsening of disability. It works by calming parts of your immune system that are attacking your nerves.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin (subcutaneous injection). You will inject it into the fatty tissue just below your skin. Common injection sites include your stomach, upper arms, upper thighs, and buttocks. Rotate your injection sites each time to avoid skin problems. Your doctor or nurse will teach you how to mix and inject the medicine properly. Always follow the preparation steps carefully — the powder must be mixed with the liquid provided before use. Never shake the mixed solution. Use each syringe only once and throw it away in a sharps container.
dosing: The usual dose is 0.25 mg (8 million IU) injected every other day (every 48 hours). To help your body get used to the medicine, your doctor may start you on a lower dose and slowly increase it over the first few weeks. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember — as long as it is not almost time for your next scheduled dose. After a missed dose, wait at least 48 hours before your next injection. Do not inject two doses at the same time or within 48 hours of each other. Try to keep a consistent every-other-day schedule.
storage: Store the unmixed powder at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not freeze the unmixed powder. After you mix the powder with the liquid, use it right away or refrigerate it and use it within 3 hours. Do not freeze the mixed solution. Keep all medicine out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol or taking other medicines that can harm your liver without talking to your doctor first, since interferon beta-1b can affect liver function. Avoid injecting into the same spot repeatedly — always rotate sites to protect your skin. Do not use the medicine if it looks discolored or contains particles. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, including vitamins and supplements, as some medicines can interact with interferon beta-1b.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: signs of liver problems such as yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, or hives; severe depression, thoughts of suicide, or unusual changes in mood or behavior; signs of infection at the injection site such as redness, swelling, pain, or skin breakdown that does not heal; chest pain or irregular heartbeat; severe flu-like symptoms that do not improve; or signs of low blood cell counts such as unusual bruising, bleeding, or frequent infections.
when_it_works: Interferon beta-1b does not cure MS, and you may not feel any different at first. It works in the background to reduce inflammation and lower the chance of relapses over time. Most people do not notice immediate effects, but the medicine is working to help protect your nervous system. It may take several months before changes are seen on MRI scans or in your relapse rate. It is important to keep using it regularly even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Interferon beta-1b may harm an unborn baby and is generally not recommended during pregnancy. Use effective birth control while taking this medicine. Older adults: Use with caution; your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver or blood problems: Regular blood tests will be needed to monitor your liver and blood cell counts. Depression: Use with extra care if you have a history of depression or mental health issues, as this medicine can worsen these conditions.
